newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: China said ready to provide N-plant to Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: China said ready to provide N-plant to Pakistan.

text.p: Pakistan said on Thursday that China was willing in principle to provide Islamabad with a second nuclear power plant, but the financing was not in place.
China is already building a 300-megawatt nuclear power plant at Chashma in the central province of Punjab under the safeguards of the International Atomic Energy Agency.

Asked if China and Pakistan had discussed the feasibility of building a "Chashma-2" during Chinese President Jiang Zemin's visit to Islamabad this week, a Foreign Ministry spokesman said: "In principle, the Chinese are willing to do so. The question of financing is yet to be resolved."
Work on the Chashma plant on the Jhelum river, 280 km (170 miles) south of Islamabad, started in 1993. It is due to be completed in 1998 and handed over to Pakistan in March 1999.
The United States urged China on Monday to halt all nuclear cooperation with Pakistan despite assurances by Beijing that it had not given nuclear technology for military purposes.
Asked to comment on the statement, the spokesman said Pakistan's peaceful nuclear cooperation with China broke no international rules and dismissed the U.S. objections.
"The remarks of the State Department (spokesman) smell of a discriminatory approach to Pakistan," he added.
He said Sino-Pakistan nuclear energy cooperation was under International Atomic Energy Agency safeguards, and any country had the right to engage in such bilateral cooperation.
"No international convention or law has been violated," he said. "No country should object to this."
A Chinese official accompanying Jiang said on Sunday that Beijing would continue its cooperation with Islamabad "in the utilisation of nuclear energy for peaceful purposes".

Pakistan, like its traditional rival India, has not signed the nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. The United States considers both coutries "threshold nuclear powers" that could quickly assemble nuclear weapons.
Washington and Beijing held lengthy talks earlier this year on sales by a Chinese firm of ring magnets, which can be used in nuclear weapons production, to Pakistan.
U.S. officials eventually accepted assurances by the Chinese government that it had not known of the sale. Beijing pledged in May that it would make no further such transfers.

Contravention by Beijing of U.S. laws through missile or nuclear technology sales could entail the imposition of U.S. sanctions on China. U.S. press reports, denied by Beijing, have repeatedly alleged that such sales have taken place.
